chunks: "NAND is the universal gate, and NOR is too. Universal means you can build any logic function using only that gate.
To prove it for NAND, I just need to show I can make NOT, AND and OR, since those three can build everything.
NOT: tie both NAND inputs together, so the output is the complement of A. AND: NAND followed by that inverter, two gates.
OR: invert each input with a NAND, then NAND them, which is De Morgan: NOT of A and NOT of B, NANDed, gives A or B. Three gates.
From there NOR is four gates, and XOR is four NAND gates in a neat pattern.
NOR works the same way by duality: NOT is a NOR with tied inputs, OR is NOR plus an inverter, and AND is the NOR of the two inverted inputs.
AND and OR on their own are not universal because neither can invert. You need some form of inversion.
In practice NAND is the one people prefer in CMOS: a NAND has the series stack in the NMOS, which is the faster device, so it's smaller and faster than a NOR.

Real chips don't literally use one gate type, but the standard-cell libraries are heavy on NAND, and knowing universality is also handy on a board: if a bug needs one more gate, any spare NAND from a 7400 package can do the job."
